articles.title: Tomatoes growing vigorously: what to check
articles.summary: Separate healthy leafy growth from common watering, light and feeding problems.
articles.body:
Start with the growing point, new leaves and the compost rather than pruning at once. A tomato that has firm green leaves, a sturdy stem and a growing tip is often simply growing well.

LIGHT AND TEMPERATURE
Tomatoes need a bright position. In a dim greenhouse, stems may become long and weak as they reach for light. Ventilate on warm days; a closed greenhouse can become excessively hot. Protect plants from cold nights and sudden temperature swings.

WATER AND FEED
Keep the root ball evenly moist, then let excess water drain. Repeated drying followed by heavy watering can split fruit and contribute to blossom-end problems. Once the first truss begins to set fruit, use a tomato feed according to its label. Too much high-nitrogen feed can favour leaves over flowers; do not add extra feed as a guess.

SIDE-SHOOTS
For a cordon variety, remove small shoots that grow in the angle between a leaf and the main stem. Bush varieties are grown differently and generally should not be trained as a single cordon. Check the seed packet before removing healthy branches.

FLOWERS NOT SETTING
Gently tap flowering trusses in still greenhouse air to help release pollen. Keep the greenhouse ventilated, and check that flowers are not being exposed to persistent heat or cold.

WEEKLY CHECK
Look under leaves for pests, check that ties are not constricting stems, water the soil rather than soaking foliage, and remove only damaged leaves or cordon side-shoots. Ask for a close photo and the variety if leaves are curling, mottled or spotted; those signs need a more specific diagnosis.

articles.title: Hardening off seedlings
articles.summary: Acclimatise indoor-grown plants gradually before moving them outdoors.
articles.body:
Hardening off reduces the shock caused by wind, bright sun and cooler nights. Begin when seedlings are healthy and large enough to handle, and use the local forecast rather than a fixed calendar date.

1. On a mild day, place plants outside in a sheltered, shaded spot for one to two hours. Bring them back indoors afterwards.
2. Repeat over roughly 7 to 10 days, extending the time outside and introducing a little gentle morning sun.
3. Keep trays watered; small cells dry quickly outdoors. Protect them from strong wind, heavy rain, slugs and cold nights.
4. Leave them outside overnight only when the crop can tolerate the forecast temperature and no cold spell is expected. Tender crops such as tomatoes and courgettes need more protection than hardy brassicas.
5. Plant out into prepared soil or a suitable container, water in, and protect from wind while roots establish.

Do not harden off wilted, recently potted or diseased seedlings. If leaves scorch or plants collapse, return them to bright shade and slow the transition.

articles.title: A practical compost routine
articles.summary: Balance moist green material with dry, airy browns and keep the heap covered.
articles.body:
A useful home compost heap needs a mixture of moist nitrogen-rich material and dry carbon-rich material, plus air and moderate moisture. Grass clippings, vegetable peelings and coffee grounds are greens. Torn cardboard, dry leaves and straw are browns.

BUILD THE HEAP
Add a variety of greens and browns in thin layers. Tear or chop bulky material so it breaks down more evenly. Keep a stash of dry browns beside the bin for wet kitchen waste. Cover the top to limit rain and discourage pests.

CHECK THE MOISTURE
The heap should feel like a wrung-out sponge. If it is wet, compacted or smells sour, mix in dry browns and turn it to introduce air. If it is dry and inactive, add water gradually while turning.

WHAT TO LEAVE OUT
Avoid meat, fish, dairy, pet waste and cooked oily food in an ordinary open garden heap; they can attract pests and create odours. Follow the compost-bin maker's guidance for any enclosed system.

USE
Finished compost is dark, crumbly and smells earthy, though small woody pieces may remain. Screen those out or return them to the heap. Use mature compost as a soil improver or mulch; it is not a complete fertiliser for every crop.

articles.title: Irish lamb and potato stew
articles.summary: A gentle one-pot family stew with lamb, onion, carrots and potatoes.
articles.body:
Serves 4 | Preparation 20 minutes | Cooking about 1 hour 45 minutes | Easy

INGREDIENTS
700 g stewing lamb, cut into bite-sized pieces; 1 tablespoon neutral oil; 2 onions, sliced; 3 carrots, cut into chunks; 700 g floury potatoes, peeled and cut into large chunks; 750 ml unsalted stock or water; 2 bay leaves; 2 tablespoons chopped parsley; black pepper. Add salt carefully if using salted stock.

METHOD
1. Heat the oven to 160 C (140 C fan). Pat the lamb dry. Brown it in batches in a heavy oven-safe pot with the oil; avoid crowding so it colours instead of steams.
2. Return the lamb to the pot. Add onions, carrots, bay leaves and stock. Bring just to a simmer, cover and cook in the oven for 45 minutes.
3. Add potatoes, cover again and cook until the lamb is tender and the potatoes are cooked, about 50 to 60 minutes. Check the liquid occasionally; add a little hot water if the pot is becoming dry.
4. Taste, season with pepper and salt if needed, then stir through parsley. Rest for 10 minutes before serving.

SERVE AND ADAPT
Serve hot with parsley and crusty bread. For a thicker broth, gently press a few cooked potato pieces against the side of the pot. Do not vigorously stir or the potatoes may break up.

STORAGE AND SAFETY
Cool leftovers promptly, refrigerate in a covered container and use within 3 days. Reheat until steaming hot throughout. Keep raw lamb separate from ready-to-eat food and wash hands and utensils after handling it.

articles.title: Sekeli-style pork and sauerkraut goulash
articles.summary: A tangy, slow-cooked Central European stew, traditionally served with bread or potato dumplings.
articles.body:
Serves 4 | Preparation 20 minutes | Cooking 1 hour 30 minutes | Easy

INGREDIENTS
600 g pork shoulder, in 2 cm cubes; 1 tablespoon oil; 2 onions, finely chopped; 2 teaspoons sweet paprika; 500 g sauerkraut, drained and rinsed if very sour; 250 ml water or unsalted stock; 1 bay leaf; 150 g sour cream, plus extra to serve; black pepper. Salt only after tasting.

METHOD
1. Warm the oil in a heavy pot. Brown the pork in batches, then set it aside.
2. Cook the onions over medium-low heat until soft. Take the pot off the heat, stir in paprika, then add a splash of water so the paprika does not scorch.
3. Return the pork. Add sauerkraut, bay leaf and remaining water. Bring to a gentle simmer, cover and cook for about 75 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the pork is tender. Add a little water if needed.
4. Remove the pot from the heat. Stir a few spoonfuls of hot cooking liquid into the sour cream, then stir this mixture back into the pot. Warm gently without boiling. Season with pepper and salt only if needed.

SERVE
Serve with bread or potato dumplings, as Bruno prefers. Boiling after adding sour cream can cause it to split, so keep the heat gentle.

LEFTOVERS
Refrigerate promptly and use within 3 days. Reheat until steaming hot throughout; add a splash of water if the stew has thickened.

articles.title: Tomato and red lentil soup
articles.summary: An inexpensive pantry soup with soft red lentils and a bright finish of lemon.
articles.body:
Serves 4 | Preparation 10 minutes | Cooking 30 minutes | Easy

INGREDIENTS
1 tablespoon olive oil; 1 onion, chopped; 1 carrot, diced; 2 garlic cloves, chopped; 1 teaspoon ground cumin; 200 g red lentils, rinsed; 400 g chopped tomatoes; 900 ml vegetable stock or water; 1 lemon; black pepper.

METHOD
1. Warm the oil in a saucepan. Cook onion and carrot for 6 to 8 minutes until soft. Stir in garlic and cumin for 30 seconds.
2. Add rinsed lentils, tomatoes and stock. Bring to a boil, then lower the heat and simmer uncovered for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the lentils are soft. Add water if you prefer a thinner soup.
3. Blend part or all of the soup, taking care with hot liquid, or leave it chunky. Add black pepper and lemon juice to taste.

SERVING AND VARIATIONS
Serve with bread and a spoon of plain yoghurt. Add chopped spinach for the final few minutes if you have it. For a milder soup, use less cumin and omit the lemon.

STORAGE
Cool promptly, refrigerate and use within 3 days. Reheat until bubbling and steaming throughout.

articles.title: A safe weekly bathroom routine
articles.summary: Work from clean areas to dirty areas and use one labelled product at a time.
articles.body:
NEED
Microfibre cloths, a non-scratch sponge, a bathroom cleaner suitable for the surfaces, toilet cleaner, gloves if the product label recommends them, and a dry cloth. Open a window or run the extractor. Read each product label.

ORDER
1. Put away toiletries and remove towels. Apply toilet cleaner as directed and leave it for the labelled contact time.
2. Dust or wipe the mirror and higher surfaces first. Clean the sink and taps with a product suitable for their finish; rinse residue and dry metal fittings.
3. Clean shower walls and tray using a compatible product. Do not use abrasive pads on acrylic, plated or coated finishes. Rinse well so cleaner does not remain on the surface.
4. Clean the toilet last with a separate cloth. Wipe the handle and nearby touch points. Wash cloths after use and wash your hands.

CHEMICAL SAFETY
Never mix cleaning products. In particular, bleach must not be mixed with acids such as vinegar, descaler or toilet cleaner, or with ammonia-containing products; dangerous gases can form. Keep products in their original labelled containers and away from children and pets. If a strong smell or irritation occurs, leave the area and ventilate it.

articles.title: Choosing and fitting a wall fixing
articles.summary: Identify the wall type and load before choosing a plug, anchor or screw.
articles.body:
First identify the wall: solid masonry, plaster over masonry, or a hollow stud wall need different fixings. Check the item weight and the fixing maker's stated load for that wall material. A plasterboard plug is not automatically suitable for a heavy shelf.

1. Check for pipes and cables with a suitable detector and review what may run behind the wall. Do not drill where you cannot make a safe assessment.
2. Mark the fixing points and check level. Use eye protection and the correct drill bit for the wall and anchor.
3. Drill to the depth and diameter specified by the fixing maker. Keep the drill square to the surface and avoid enlarging the hole.
4. Fit the plug or hollow-wall anchor as instructed, then tighten the screw until secure. Do not overtighten a plasterboard anchor.
5. Test gently before loading the fitting. If the wall crumbles, the anchor spins or the load is uncertain, stop and choose a safer fixing or get qualified help.

Do not drill into a wall that may contain mains wiring or plumbing unless you can establish a safe route. Structural alterations, gas work and mains electrical work need a qualified professional.

articles.title: Preparing clay by wedging
articles.summary: A simple check and preparation routine before hand-building or throwing.
articles.body:
Wedging makes a workable lump more even and helps remove soft and firm pockets. Follow the clay supplier's safety guidance and keep clay dust out of the air: clean damp, never sweep or sand dry clay.

1. Use a clean, non-porous wedging surface. Cut the clay block with a wire and check for hard inclusions or dried edges.
2. For a small amount, use a consistent spiral or ram's-head motion: press the clay forward and down, fold it back over itself, then repeat while rotating the lump. Keep the movement controlled and avoid trapping large air pockets.
3. If the clay is too soft, cut it into slabs and let it stiffen on a clean absorbent board. If too firm, wedge in a small amount of the same clay body that has been softened; do not add an unknown amount of water to the surface.
4. Cut through the lump with a wire to inspect its consistency. If it is still marbled with very different moisture levels, continue wedging or let it equalise in a sealed bag.

Wedging does not make clay safe for every project or firing. Keep clay bodies labelled and follow the clay and glaze manufacturer's instructions for drying and firing.

articles.title: Check compatibility before changing a console
articles.summary: Record the exact model and firmware before following any device-specific setup guide.
articles.body:
Compatibility depends on the exact console model, hardware revision, region and installed firmware. A guide for a similar-looking model may not apply. Exploit and homebrew compatibility can change with firmware updates, so treat current compatibility as online-only until checked against the project maintainers' latest information.

BEFORE YOU START
1. Photograph the model label and record the full model number, region and current system software version. Do not post serial numbers publicly.
2. Read the original guide from its maintainer from beginning to end. Confirm that its model and firmware range match your device exactly.
3. Back up saves and any data the supported system tools allow. Confirm you can restore the backup before making a change.
4. Use only legitimate homebrew and game content you are entitled to use. Do not download commercial game images from unofficial sources.
5. Avoid downgrades, firmware files or steps whose source and device match you cannot verify. An interrupted or incompatible procedure may make the console unusable.

If the device's compatibility details do not match, stop and seek a current, device-specific source. This guide is evergreen safety advice, not a claim that any particular firmware can be modified today.

articles.title: Monthly bill review checklist
articles.summary: A private checklist for checking due dates and recording what you verified.
articles.body:
Once a month, review the bill or provider's own statement and record only what you need: provider, amount, due date, and a reminder of the next action. A saved reminder does not mean a payment has been made.

1. Compare the due date and amount against the latest statement, not a previous month.
2. Note whether the amount is fixed or variable and whether a direct debit or manual payment is expected.
3. If something looks wrong, contact the provider using contact information from its official statement or website. Do not rely on a link in an unexpected message.
4. After checking or paying, update your own note with the date and confirmation reference you choose to keep.
5. Keep account numbers, payment card details and one-time codes out of general notes and AI prompts.

Suric does not connect to providers, make payments or verify account balances. Use the provider's authenticated channel for those tasks.

articles.title: Compare online options without losing the details
articles.summary: Record total cost, fit and return terms from the retailer before deciding.
articles.body:
For each option, record the exact model or item, total delivered price, delivery estimate, dimensions, warranty and return conditions. Include the date you checked each detail: retailer pages and stock can change.

1. Decide which features are essential and which are preferences.
2. Check the retailer's full delivered price, including delivery and any required accessories.
3. Confirm the model number, size and compatibility from the manufacturer or retailer listing.
4. Read the return and warranty terms before purchase, especially for opened or made-to-order items.
5. Save the source link and your own notes, then recheck live information at the retailer before deciding.

Suric stores the details you enter. It does not fetch pages, verify current prices or stock, endorse a seller, or place an order.
